title: One long vendor file, five products, four units: build the daily crack table

explain.prompt: The trader wants “the crack history on one sheet”. In 4–6 sentences with your numbers: what the key of this file is, which conversions you applied, and how you treated gaps — compare leaving them blank, dropping incomplete dates and forward-filling, and say why the right choice is not the same for every gap.
rubric: The key is (date, product): 7,893 rows, 3 exact copies dropped, and an assertion that no (date, product) pair is left with two different prices — a conflicting pair would need a decision, not a silent drop.

Units are converted row by row from the unit column: USD/gal × 42, USc/gal × 0.42 (ULSD was quoted in cents until end-2020, 1,009 rows), USD/t ÷ density (gasoil 7.45, jet 7.88 bbl/t). Converting by product name alone would mis-scale 1,009 ULSD prices by 100.

Gaps in a long file are absent rows: they only appear as NaN after the pivot. UK holidays remove Brent, gasoil and jet; US holidays remove ULSD and RBOB; jet starts on 1 Mar 2018; the last three jet days are not yet published.

A frozen gasoil feed (the same price six sessions in a row, 8–15 Oct 2018) is blanked after its first value: forward-filling would have turned it into eight days of a stale price and moved the October mean crack from 17.98 to 18.56.

Dropping every incomplete date keeps 1,308 of 1,671 dates — it throws away 2017 entirely for the gasoil crack because jet did not exist. Forward-filling Brent across a UK holiday would compute 30 ULSD cracks against yesterday's Brent: two different days in one spread.

Decision: leave gaps blank, crack only where both legs exist, and fill nothing at this stage; a single unit error (RBOB 2019-05-14 sent in cents, 8,732 $/bbl) is still in the data and is the job of 2.3.
